docs.title: specs
docs.text:
specs() -> dict[str, ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec | SpecSource]

A fresh name -> spec dict - the shape adapters already accept.

Each spec as registered, so an object with as_kernel_spec() is handed back as itself; every entry point here takes it as it is.

Pass registry.specs() wherever a dict[str, spec] goes today. Mutating the returned dict does not affect the registry.

docs.title: RegisteredSpec dataclass
docs.text:
A spec under its canonical name, with free-form tags.

The value type held by SpecRegistry. It carries only the part of an operation that is invariant across transports - which spec, what it is called, and how it is grouped. Per-transport configuration (an HTTP view's URL kwargs, an MCP tool's annotations, an agent adapter's own metadata) stays at the binding that configures it, not here.

Fields:

  • name - the canonical name for this operation. Unique within the registry that holds it; two independent registries are separate namespaces and may reuse a name.
  • spec - a ServiceSpec (a write) or a SelectorSpec (a read), or a SpecSource that compiles to one, kept as registered: a transport reads the spec it runs through kernel_spec, and the object itself is still there to be asked what only it knows. The kind is deliberately not stored as its own field: it is derived by isinstance on the compiled spec wherever it is needed, so a stored discriminator can never drift from the object it describes.
  • tags - a frozen set of free-form labels used to derive filtered views (registry.by_tag("public")). Tags carry boolean-ish facts - "read", "admin", "destructive" - that every transport can interpret in its own vocabulary.

docs.title: agent_contract property
docs.text:
agent_contract: Any

The registered object's own agent_contract(), or None when it has none.

Read-only, and never a field: a declaration lives on the spec, never on the registry entry, so nothing is passed here and the entry only asks. A ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec has none and answers None; an object registered from djangorestframework-services answers the contract its current release builds from what the spec declares, for the transports published against that release. Typed Any because the value is that object's, of a type this package does not name. Asked on every read, so it is never stale.

docs.title: capability_manifest
docs.text:
capability_manifest(
    registry: SpecRegistry,
    *,
    schema_registry: JsonSchemaRegistry = DEFAULT_JSON_SCHEMA_REGISTRY,
) -> dict[str, Any]

Describe every operation in registry: what exists and what shape it takes.

The surface a transport already derives piecemeal -- an MCP tool list, an agent toolset's descriptions, a frontend's action menu -- as one JSON-native document, derived from the registry rather than written by hand:

{
    "version": 1,
    "dialect": "rest_framework_services.jsonschema/1",
    "operations": [
        {
            "name": "refund_order",
            "kind": "mutation",
            "tags": ["admin", "write"],
            "idempotent": True,
            "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {...}},
            "output_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {...}},
            "guards": [{"source": "orders.permissions.IsSupport"}],
            "affordances": [
                {
                    "code": "order_shipped",
                    "reason": "A shipped order cannot be cancelled.",
                    "scope": "row",
                }
            ],
        },
        ...
    ],
    "unguarded": [],
}

It names no principal and decides nothing, deliberately. It is the same for every caller, so it says which guards an operation carries and never what they grant: a permission class is code, and nothing short of running it against a principal answers that. A reader that understands a declarative policy can layer a decision onto each operation; this document is what such a reader starts from. For the same reason it is not a document to serve to a client -- it enumerates operations a given caller may be unable to see at all.

Keys, per operation:

  • name -- the registry name, which is the operation's identity across transports.
  • kind -- "mutation" for a ServiceSpec, "query" for a SelectorSpec, derived by type exactly as the registry derives it.
  • tags -- sorted, so two manifests of one registry are byte-identical.
  • idempotent -- ServiceSpec.idempotent as declared, None included: silence is not a claim, and a reader must be able to tell it from a declared False. Always None on a query, which has no such declaration -- its kind already says it changes nothing.
  • input_schema / output_schema -- exactly what spec_to_json_schema derives for each phase, so the document carries this package's schema dialect rather than a second one; output_schema is None where no output is declared. A single-row output_schema admits null where can_present_nothing says dispatch may present None. dialect names that policy at the top level.
  • guards -- one {"source": <dotted class path>} per permission class, in declaration order. Always a list: a SpecRegistry refuses a spec that declares none, so [] is a declared "no permissions".
  • affordances -- one {"code": ..., "reason": ..., "scope": ...} per Affordance a mutation declares, in declaration order: the codes a call can be refused with, and the sentence each refusal says. scope is "row" for a condition on the row, which is answered per object, and "operation" for a callable one, which is answered without a row and so can decide whether the operation is offered at all. None where nothing is declared, and always on a query. The code here is the same code a rendered object's affordances answer carries and a 409 body names, and the reason is the same declared sentence those carry beside it, so a model reading the manifest learns what each refusal will say before it meets one. Both are declarations about the operation, never a row's state.

unguarded is unguarded_specs over the same registry: the operations whose permission_classes is None, which have nothing to inherit off HTTP. A SpecRegistry refuses such a spec when it is registered, so on a registry that holds only what it accepted the list is empty; it stays for the readers that expect the key.

Pure: it reads declarations and never the database, so building it at startup, in a management command, or in a test costs the schema walk and nothing else.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default registry SpecRegistry

The operations to describe, in registration order.

required schema_registry JsonSchemaRegistry

Consumer rules for custom field / filter / Python types, forwarded to the schema derivation -- the same object a transport passes to spec_to_json_schema, so the manifest and the transport describe a custom field identically.

DEFAULT_JSON_SCHEMA_REGISTRY

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

registry is not a SpecRegistry. A bare name -> spec mapping has no tags, so every operation would be reported untagged -- a manifest that is quietly smaller than the one a registry produces.

docs.title: OfflineContract dataclass
docs.text:
The declarations an off-HTTP caller needs and an HTTP one never does.

Over HTTP this is all free. A nested route's captures reach a spec through view.kwargs because the URLconf declared them; read-shaping params reach a serializer through request.query_params because the query string carried them. A spec mounted on a view is already complete.

Off HTTP there is no route and no query string, so somebody has to say what they would have contained. That is what this is: not a missing part of the operation, but a description of the request that is not there.

UrlKwarg("project_pk") means "when there is no URL, synthesise this view kwarg from a caller-supplied argument" -- a sentence with no meaning on a transport that has a URL. Which is exactly why it does not belong on the spec itself: the spec would carry a field HTTP must ignore, and a second declaration of a fact the URLconf already owns, pointing the other way.

It belongs to the entry rather than to any one transport because every off-HTTP transport needs the identical answer. MCP and an in-process Pydantic-AI toolset synthesise the same absent request for the same operation; a project running both used to declare it twice, in two shapes, with nothing comparing them.

Deliberately not a home for bounds or strictness -- result-size caps, page ceilings, timeouts, unknown-argument policy. Those legitimately differ between a publicly exposed server and an in-process toolset, and one shared number would be a regression rather than a simplification. This carries only what cannot differ.

Sorting is absent for the same reason from the other direction: it is declared by the spec's own filter_set, which is already read by every transport, so it needs no second home.

Transports read this as a default. A mount may still override it, and one that says nothing inherits it.

docs.title: field_audiences class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
field_audiences: Mapping[str, FieldMarking] | None = None

Per-tool overrides layered over the output serializer's own markings.

Here rather than at a mount because FieldAudience already settles the question: the axis is audience, not protocol -- an MCP server and an in-process toolset want the same thing as each other, and something different from a browser. If the two are one audience, an override of what that audience sees cannot legitimately differ between them.

It also belongs at the same level as the thing it overrides. The baseline is the serializer's own FieldMarking markings, which are spec-level and read by every transport; declaring the baseline once and the override per mount is what let one spec project a different field set depending on which transport served it -- a field hidden for one agent audience left visible to the other, with nothing comparing them.

docs.title: Protocols
docs.text: Each Protocol is parameterised on input / instance / result types only; **extras is typed Any. Strict-typed extras live on the user's function signature via **extras: Unpack[YourKw] — see Typing services and selectors for the full pattern.

docs.title: Selector
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Any callable returning a queryset, a list or one object.

The loosest description of a SelectorSpec's selector: dispatch binds it from the keywords it declares, drawn from the keyword pool and the reads the spec declares, so no signature is imposed and conforming is optional. For a typed result, use ListSelector or RetrieveSelector.

Runtime-checkable, and an isinstance check asks only whether the object is callable: an async def passes it too, so it cannot tell the two kinds apart.

docs.title: AsyncSelector
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

The async def sibling of Selector.

A SelectorSpec's selector may be async def, and adispatch awaits it. To a type checker the two Protocols differ in the return, an awaitable here. An isinstance check cannot tell them apart, since both ask only whether the object is callable; is_async is the run-time question.

docs.title: ListSelector
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol[ResultT]

The structural shape of the selector of a LIST SelectorSpec.

It returns the rows, a queryset or any other iterable; a queryset is what the spec's shaping (extend_queryset and its peers) can act on. Every keyword arrives through **extras.

See CreateService for **extras and strictly typed extras.

docs.title: RetrieveSelector
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol[ResultT]

The structural shape of the selector of a RETRIEVE SelectorSpec.

It returns the one row, or None for a row that is not there, which dispatch answers as not-found unless the spec declares allow_none. A selector returning a queryset, which dispatch collapses to its one row, binds ResultT to the queryset's type. The lookup the spec reads - typically pk - arrives through **extras with every other keyword.

See CreateService for **extras and strictly typed extras.

docs.title: call_selector
docs.text:
call_selector(
    selector: Callable[..., ResultT], *, request: Request, **extras: Any
) -> ResultT

Invoke selector with the framework's kwargs pool.

request is required; user is derived from request.user, and view is the view DRF recorded on the request it built (a plain HttpRequest records none). extras are spread last, so a key in them replaces either seed; call_service drops such a key instead. Async selectors are bridged via async_to_sync.

docs.title: acall_selector async
docs.text:
acall_selector(
    selector: Callable[..., ResultT] | Callable[..., Awaitable[ResultT]],
    *,
    request: Request,
    **extras: Any,
) -> ResultT

Invoke selector from async code with the framework's kwargs pool.

Async selectors are awaited; sync selectors are called inline.

docs.title: utils
docs.text: Internal selector dispatch helpers (sync + async).

docs.title: apply_queryset_shaping
docs.text:
apply_queryset_shaping(
    qs: Any,
    view: Any,
    request: Request,
    *,
    select_related: Any,
    prefetch_related: Any,
    annotations: Any,
    extend_queryset: Any,
    filter_set: Any = None,
    filter_data: Any = None,
    source_label: str,
) -> Any

Apply the five shaping fields to qs, through the kernel's shape_queryset.

drfs' signature over django-service-specs' shaping, for a caller holding a view and a request rather than a spec: the fields become a kernel SelectorSpec (with a stand-in selector it never runs), and view, request and the filter's arguments its pool. The order is the kernel's: the declarative fields first (in declaration order), then extend_queryset, so the user callable always sees the fully statically-shaped queryset, and finally filter_set, so filtering composes with shaping and runs before the retrieve .first() materialization the caller does next.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default extend_queryset Any

Called as extend_queryset(qs, view, request), by position, as it always was; the kernel binds its own by name.

required filter_set Any

A django-filter FilterSet, validated before .qs is read, and handed request through its constructor, so a request-scoped one sees the self.request it would behind DjangoFilterBackend.

None filter_data Any

The mapping the filter's arguments are read from, each of its filters' names and nothing else. None falls back to request.query_params, the HTTP view path. A QueryDict is read flat as dispatch reads a query string: a repeated key as a list where the filter takes several values, and each value coerced to the type the filter declares.

None source_label str

Named in the misconfiguration error to point at the offending callable ("SelectorSpec.selector" vs "ServiceSpec.output_selector_spec.selector").

required

Returns:

Type Description Any

The shaped queryset, or qs unchanged when nothing is configured.

Raises:

Type Description ImproperlyConfigured

Shaping is configured but qs is not a Django queryset; filter_set is not a django-filter FilterSet (one duck-typed on (data, queryset) -> .qs is refused); or extend_queryset answered with an awaitable.

InvalidArguments

The kernel's, where filter_set refused its data or a value no integer column can hold, keyed as the FilterSet keys its errors. It reaches the caller as the kernel raised it, not as DRF's ValidationError: nothing here translates it, so a caller inside a DRF view that wants a 400 translates it itself.

docs.title: check_view_object_permissions
docs.text:
check_view_object_permissions(spec: Any, context: Any, *, instance: Any = None) -> None

TargetGuard running DRF's object-permission check for an HTTP view.

The HTTP counterpart of enforce_permissions: off HTTP a transport enforces spec.permission_classes itself, while a DRF view has already instantiated them and exposes check_object_permissions. Both plug into the same on_target_resolved seam, so the core stays authz-agnostic on every transport.

Gated on Model, like enforce_permissions: the core fires this hook on the LIST branch too, with the resolved queryset, and object permissions are per-row. None — a create, or a bulk list payload — is skipped too.

docs.title: dispatch_selector_for_spec
docs.text:
dispatch_selector_for_spec(view: Any, spec: SelectorSpec[Any, Any]) -> Any

End-to-end dispatch for one SelectorSpec call from a DRF view.

Resolves the view's get_selector_kwargs / get_<action>_selector_kwargs chain into a ViewHooks carrier, hands off to the one dispatch_spec core, and translates the neutral DispatchResult into the view-layer contract: a RETRIEVE that resolved nothing raises NotFound, unless the spec sets allow_none=True (then None, and the retrieve views render 200 + JSON null). SelectorKind.LIST returns the shaped queryset.

The request is no argument mapping. Off HTTP the flat params mapping is the argument channel; over HTTP it is empty, and a selector's arguments come from what the spec declares it reads: a route capture of one of its reads or a declared UrlKwarg from view.kwargs, a declared QueryParam from the query string, and the hook chain's values. The query string reaches the filter_set as filter_data, restricted to the names the filter reads, so it feeds the filter without widening the argument channel.

There is deliberately no extra_url_kwargs parameter: the core reads view.kwargs itself, for the names the spec reads and the ones its callables mark NotClientInput, and a capture named like a seed of the call never replaces the seed, so a nested route like /users/<user>/posts/ cannot let the captured value shadow the authenticated user (test_url_kwarg_cannot_shadow_the_authenticated_user_over_http). Taking the mapping from a caller would reopen that.

The caller must check spec.selector is not None first and fall back to vanilla DRF otherwise.

docs.title: Service specs on the kernel
docs.text:
A ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec declared here is a source for django-service-specs: it answers as_kernel_spec(), so the kernel's kernel_spec(spec) compiles it once, and dispatch, authorize and a SpecRegistry take the drfs spec itself. Every drfs field lands on a kernel seat or is named below as the HTTP views' own.

A many spec's list is judged differently by the two routes. dispatch_spec judges the list on the rows sent: where the list as sent is within its length bounds, a row that is no object is refused alone, and the list's validate() is left to the rows as sent. The kernel's dispatch called directly on a drfs spec has no such body to hold the rows and judges the list on the rows that survived, in the kernel's own classes and words: [good, 1] under a minimum of two answers row 1's Expected an object. beside Ensure this field has at least 2 elements., and a list-level validate() runs over the rows left.

docs.title: What a spec declares for a caller off HTTP
docs.text:
Over HTTP a URLconf captures a nested route's project_pk and a query string carries fields. Off HTTP somebody has to say they exist, so a spec declares them itself:

from rest_framework_services import QueryParam, SelectorKind, SelectorSpec, UrlKwarg

list_tasks = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=tasks_for_project,
    reads=[
        UrlKwarg("project_pk", type="integer", required=True),
        QueryParam("fields", description="Fields to return."),
    ],
)
  • reads: each UrlKwarg and QueryParam becomes one kernel Parameter, so it is an argument a caller sends and the schema lists. A QueryParam no callable of the call takes by name compiles to the kernel spec's shapes rather than its reads, and reaches the presenter on PresentationContext.shapes (see QueryParam). An entry of the same name as a selector parameter replaces the reflected one and keeps what that parameter requires: a read naming a parameter with no default, of the selector, a target lookup, the service or a precondition, is required too, unless the read declares a default; the compiled parameters and the kernel's input schema say so, and a parameter marked InputRequired stays required under the read. A sequence is required, and a name may be declared once. A selector taking a bare **kwargs is not handed a route capture no callable declares: declare it here or as a keyword parameter. A UrlKwarg's type has to be the one the route's converter yields: UrlKwarg("pk", type="integer") for <int:pk>/, since the default string refuses an int capture as Expected a string..
  • field_audiences: per-field markings layered over the output serializer's own. On a ServiceSpec they layer over its output selector's. A spec declaring them with no output serializer is refused at compile, with a message naming both.
  • agent_contract(): the OfflineContract these two declare, which a registry entry answers for transports that read it. None when both are empty.

docs.title: Where each field lands
docs.text:
drfs field Kernel seat permission_classes one DRFPermissionCheck; [] is Unrestricted(), and None is no permissions, which a registry refuses input_serializer validator (a SerializerValidator) output_selector_spec.output_serializer, output_serializer presenter (a SerializerPresenter) input_serializer_context the SerializerValidator's serializer_context output_selector_spec.output_serializer_context, output_serializer_context the SerializerPresenter's serializer_context partial partial, kept only with an input_serializer many, many_argument the same; the list bounds come from the serializer's ListSerializer and apply off HTTP and on an OfflineServiceView, while a live view's bulk body is bounded by the ListSerializer alone extend_queryset extend_queryset, called as extend(queryset, view, request) affordances each service's compiled spec everything else of the same name carried by name

A service with no input_serializer declares none of its own parameters, so kernel_spec(spec).parameters() lists only its target lookup's keys and its reads, and no body reaches the service's keywords. Its signature is declared only in the variant compiled for an explicit ArgumentBinding.SPREAD_AUTHOR_WINS (kernel_spec_variant(spec, spread=True)). A selector always takes its arguments from its signature, except for the names its filter_set owns. Parameters marked NotClientInput on any callable of the call are hidden. So are the names the pool fills: user, request, view, queryset, result and the rest.

parameters() is not available on every compiled spec. Where a target lookup's selector reads a name that is also a writable input field, such as renaming a row by the slug that finds it, kernel_spec(spec).parameters() and as_kernel_spec(spec).parameters() raise ImproperlyConfigured ("Parameters ['slug'] are declared by two sources"), because the kernel declares one source per name. Such a spec still registers and dispatches, and spec_to_json_schema describes it: the route's capture scopes the lookup, and the body's value is the field's.

Three reads declarations are refused with ImproperlyConfigured when the spec compiles (at registration, or whenever it is dispatched, over HTTP too), each naming the read:

  • a name the pool fills, which would never be the caller's;
  • a name the spec's service or selector, or one of its preconditions, marks NotClientInput. Dispatch hands a declared read to each of those callables by name, so the same callable would be given the client's value for a parameter it keeps the server's. The message names the callable and the mark; remove one of the two;
  • a name a writable field of the input serializer also takes, declared on the spec or on its target lookup. The body's value of that name is the field's, so the read would reach neither the service nor the lookup. The message names the read, the serializer and, where it reads the name too, the target lookup. A UrlKwarg the target lookup reads is accepted: that is the rename-by-key shape above, where the route's capture scopes the lookup. A many spec's fields are each row's, and a read-only field and a HiddenField take nothing from the body, so none is a clash: a UrlKwarg named like a HiddenField whose default reads view.kwargs is how a route capture scopes a write, and off HTTP the caller's value for it is written onto view.kwargs, where the default reads it.

A serializer whose fields cannot be read when the spec compiles - they read the request, or query a table migrate has not made yet, or a row not yet there - is taken to declare no name, so registering it at import never needs the database; the call that describes it is where such a read is refused. A many=True spec whose serializer cannot be built then compiles with no list bound of its own, and the list serializer that validates the call still holds the list to the bound it declares.

A name only a target lookup marks NotClientInput is accepted: the lookup is never handed a read it hides, so the read is the service's argument and the lookup keeps its own value.

A nested spec compiles to what the kernel runs:

  • its permission_classes are not carried;
  • an instance lookup's allow_none and output_serializer are dropped;
  • an output selector's kwargs are dropped;
  • an output selector with no selector moves its serializer onto the service spec's presenter;
  • preconditions and progress_reporter, which would never run there, are refused.

success_status, document_service_error and response_finalizer are the HTTP views' and are not compiled.

The two serializer context callables ride on the adapters and are asked when the serializer is built for a call, over DRF's own context and the view hooks dispatch_spec registers for the call; see Customise serializer context.

docs.title: The serializer as Validator and Presenter
docs.text: SerializerValidator is the kernel's Validator over an input_serializer (a DRF serializer or a dataclass): its parameters are the serializer's fields, and it validates a call with the target as instance, the call's partial, and a serializer context built for the principal, so CurrentUserDefault reads it. A HiddenField or a read-only field is not a parameter, and neither is a field named like a seed (user, result, a registered seed's name): the serializer reads it from the body, so its value lands in data and the seed keeps its own. For a request a live DRF view dispatches, the edge compiles a lenient variant (kernel_spec_variant(spec, lenient=True)) whose parameters carry their names alone, so DRF's serializer is the only validator and answers in its own words; off HTTP the parameters carry their types and the kernel checks them first. SerializerPresenter is the kernel's Presenter over an output serializer, with the spec's field_audiences layered over the serializer's own markings.

docs.title: SerializerValidator
docs.text:
Bases: Validator

A Validator whose declaration is a DRF serializer, or a dataclass read through one.

It takes what a drfs spec's input_serializer takes: a Serializer subclass, ModelSerializer and DataclassSerializer included, or a dataclass, which is validated through a DataclassSerializer exactly as drfs' dispatch validates it. Anything else is refused with ImproperlyConfigured when the Validator is built.

parameters() walks the serializer's fields, in order, as the field walk in service_specs/utils.py reads them: a nested serializer is an object with Parameters of its own, many=True and a ListField an array, a file field a file, choices with their labels; a HiddenField and a read-only field are no parameter. It is read on each call rather than when the Validator is built, because specs are built at import time, when a ModelSerializer cannot yet read its model, and so that help is rendered in the language active when it is asked for. It never queries.

validate() builds the serializer as a DRF view would:

  • over the body the call was sent, where a DRF edge call names this Validator (validator_input): the caller's own data, a QueryDict kept one, with what the edge put over it, as a DRF view's serializer was always handed request.data. Anywhere else, the kernel's checked arguments.

  • with the target as instance, so an update's uniqueness checks exclude the row being updated. The queryset a collection selector resolves is no row, so a call over one binds as a create, as drfs' dispatch binds it; the target is handed over as it is, since a serializer, unlike a ModelForm, writes nothing onto its instance while it validates.

  • partial as the call is, the context's partial, so a partial call may leave out a required field and returns only what was sent.
  • under the serializer context DRF builds on HTTP, request, format and view. The request and view the call registered as pool seeds are the serializer's own, read from ValidationContext.ambient as the kernel resolved them, and where a seed is absent or None, the entry of that name in ValidationContext.call_context. A call that carries neither gets an offline request whose user is the principal and whose data is the arguments, built by build_offline_context, so a CurrentUserDefault reads the principal and a field or a validate() reading self.context["request"] finds a request rather than a KeyError. What a registered request's user is, is the transport's to make the principal; the Validator never writes to a call's own objects. Over that, the input half of the view hooks a DRF edge carries for the call (input_view_layers), then serializer_context, the spec's own input_serializer_context, each winning on a key it shares with what it layers over (see serializer_context in service_specs/utils.py). The callable declares what it reads from the call's pool: request, view, user, call_context, a registered seed, or an argument. It is asked once per call, a many call's included, except where the call builds the serializer twice, for a body the server puts a value into or a row a target lookup resolves, and what the callable is handed differs between the two.

A refusal is one InvalidArguments, the kernel's refusal that is DRF's ValidationError as well, carrying the serializer's errors unchanged: DRF's ErrorDetail leaves, each with its code, cross-field messages under non_field_errors, and a nested list's errors in whichever shape the installed DRF writes them.

validated() hands the service what drfs' dispatch hands it: data is the serializer's validated_data - the validated mapping, or the dataclass instance a DataclassSerializer builds - and the bound serializer is bound for the call as serializer. values follow what validated_data is, as drfs' dispatch reads it: a mapping's entries, keyed as DRF keys them, by each field's source; a dataclass instance's __init__ fields, whether a dataclass was declared or a DataclassSerializer subclass was; and nothing for any other object a serializer's validate() returns, which reaches the service only as data. A key named like a seed of the call is a value only in data: DRF's HiddenField(default=CurrentUserDefault()) named user, or a key a validate() adds named result, stays in validated_data as the serializer built it, and the service's user is the call's principal, as drfs always handed them (see _unseeded). So is a key named in server_owned, the names a callable of the call marks NotClientInput, which the compiled spec hands it: the client's value is the service's in data alone, unless the edge put the server's value into the field it comes from (see _unowned). Where the edge did, that field's validation of the value the edge put is the key's value, validated on its own once the serializer has accepted the body, never read back off the body (see _server_values), whatever the field reads from the body, and whatever a later field of the same source, a source="*" nested serializer, a validate() or a to_internal_value override did to the key: it is the parameter's, by the field's source or, where that is no single key, by the field's name, and by the key an author named it under (see _handed), and it is laid back over the key in a mapping data (see _lay_back). A dataclass instance is data as built, and a many call's rows are neither validated apart nor laid back.

A partial call over a dataclass is refused, a DataclassSerializer subclass included: one builds its instance from every field, and a field a partial call left out fails as a TypeError from inside the library. supports_partial is therefore answered per instance, False for either declaration and True for any other serializer, so a spec declaring partial=True over a dataclass is refused when it is built. A partial call made on the Validator directly is refused with ImproperlyConfigured as well.

validated_many() validates a many spec's rows as DRF's own list serializer does, once: the serializer's child class under many=True (so a Meta.list_serializer_class and its list-level validate() run), with the call's context and partial flag. The one list serializer is bound for the call as serializer, data is the list of each row's validated_data and the values are the rows' values under many_argument. A refusal is an InvalidArguments whose detail keys each failing row by the index the caller's list gave it, whichever of DRF's two shapes the installed version reports item errors in, and whose list-level message sits under non_field_errors. A live view's list body (EdgeCallState.body_rows) is bound whole, every row as sent, and what the list serializer refused is also left on the edge's state as DRF reported it, for the edge to answer with as a view always did. Where the kernel refused a row the edge sent, the rows it passed are read but the list is judged as sent: its length bounds count every row sent, and its list-level validate() does not run, as DRF never runs it past a refused row.

docs.title: parameters
docs.text:
parameters() -> Parameters

The serializer's input fields, as Parameters.

Read off describe_serializer: inside an edge call, the serializer the call builds once and validates with, so a serializer that queries as it is built queries once in the call (test_its_queries_run_once_off_http); outside one, a serializer built afresh for each read, as a schema or a registration reads it.

A field named like a seed of the call is no parameter: one of the dispatcher's own names (RESERVED_POOL_SEEDS, test_a_writable_field_named_user_validates_off_http) and the serializer this Validator binds (BOUND, test_an_input_field_named_serializer_validates_into_data) always, and each of excluded, which the DRF edge compiles with the names the call's registered seeds take (test_a_writable_field_named_like_a_registered_seed_validates). The kernel refuses a parameter a seed occupies, where a serializer was always free to declare such a field: the client sent its value, the serializer validated it into data, and the seed kept its own. So the field is the serializer's alone, read from the body the edge hands it (validator_input), and never meets the seed in the call's pool.

lenient declares each field by name alone - any value, optional, nullable - so the kernel's shape check passes every value through and the serializer is the one to answer it, as a live DRF view's request always was answered (kernel_spec_variant(lenient=True)).

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
validate(arguments: Mapping[str, Any], context: ValidationContext) -> dict[str, Any]

The validated values, keyed by source, or InvalidArguments carrying DRF's detail.

docs.title: validated
docs.text:
validated(arguments: Mapping[str, Any], context: ValidationContext) -> Validated

The values, validated_data as the call's data, and the bound serializer.

docs.title: validated_many
docs.text:
validated_many(
    rows: Mapping[int, Mapping[str, Any]],
    context: ValidationContext,
    *,
    many_argument: str,
) -> Validated

The rows validated once as DRF's list serializer, the one serializer bound for the call.

docs.title: SerializerPresenter
docs.text:
Bases: Presenter

An operation's output declared as a DRF serializer, rendered through it.

``output()`` reads the serializer's fields into the kernel's
[`Output`][django_service_specs.output.output.Output], in declaration order,
the way drfs' own output schema and audience walk read them:

- A ``write_only`` field is never rendered, so it is not declared.
- **Type**: JSON's own, with ``decimal``, ``date-time`` and ``date`` as
  formats. A nested serializer is an object carrying its own ``Output``; a
  ``many=True`` serializer, and a ``ListField`` whose child is one, is an
  array of that ``Output``; a ``MultipleChoiceField`` is an array of its
  choices. A field DRF gives no type, a
  ``SerializerMethodField`` or a ``JSONField`` say, is declared ``any``,
  so a schema describes it with no ``type`` rather than as a string it may
  not be.

  • Label: the author's, when one was written. DRF derives Vat id from vat_id when none was, and that is None here, as it is no title in drfs' schema.

    • Choices: every (value, display) pair a ChoiceField holds, typed by the values when they share a type.
    • Presence: always_present is true where DRF is bound to emit the key: a required field, one with a default, and one allowing null. A read-only field with neither is dropped when DRF cannot read it. Under shaped=True, no field at any depth is: the spec compiles a shape, an argument such as a fields selector that the serializer reads off the request, and a key is always present only if it is present under every value the caller may send. A drfs QueryParam declares no choices, so the values are any string, and which keys each one drops is the serializer's to decide when it renders, so the keys present under all of them are none that can be named. The default, False, is the presence above.
    • Marking: the FieldMarking found in the field's style, under MARKING or any other key, and a value under MARKING that is not one refused, as drfs' walk reads it. Nested outputs carry their own.

    field_audiences is the spec's own output declaration, a field name to a FieldMarking, layered over the serializer's markings at the top level only, as drfs' overrides= always has been. The layered marking is the compiled OutputField.marking, which is the seat audience_projection_for_spec reads, so every engine projects the one declaration with no overrides=, which stays a mount's. A name that is no output field is refused when the output is read: a hidden marking that silently applies to nothing is a field shown to an agent.

    presented(value, context) is what the kernel's present asks for: the serializer's .data for one value, under the serializer context derived from the call's PresentationContext. The request and view the call registered as pool seeds, read from ambient, are the serializer's own, and where a seed is absent or None, the entry of that name in call_context; a call that carries neither gets an offline request whose user is the principal, so a SerializerMethodField reading self.context["request"].user renders for the principal the call ran for, and whose query string is the call's shapes, so a serializer reading a fields selector off request.query_params finds the one the caller sent. A request the call carries is left as it is. A list result is presented row by row by the kernel's present, each row with the same context, which is what a many=True render is. Over that, the output half of the view hooks a DRF edge adds to the result's context (output_view_layers), resolved with the value, then serializer_context, the spec's own output_serializer_context, each winning on a key it shares with what it layers over (see serializer_context in service_specs/utils.py). The callable declares what it reads from the call's pool, request, view, user or a registered seed, and the value being presented under value_keyword: result for a service's output, instance for a retrieve. It is asked once per value presented, so for a list or a many service's output once per row, and no keyword names the row then (value_keyword is None), nor is the view's hook handed it: the kernel presents a set row by row, and the whole set a callable may declare, a list's page or a many output's result, is never in hand here.

    present(value) is the context-free form, and delegates to presented(value, None): a None context is the serializer context drfs describes a serializer with (request, view and format present, each None), so a get_fields reading self.context["request"] neither raises there nor sees a principal. It is what a DispatchResult a transport built by hand is presented with, and with no call to resolve it against, serializer_context is not asked (test_present_with_no_call_runs_no_callable).

    A dataclass type is read and rendered through the DataclassSerializer drfs renders it with, and a BaseSerializer that is not a Serializer declares no fields, so its output is empty while it still presents.

docs.title: output
docs.text:
output() -> Output

The serializer's fields as an Output, with field_audiences layered on. Never queries.

docs.title: present
docs.text:
present(value: Any) -> Any

One value as the serializer's .data, with no call to render for.

docs.title: presented
docs.text:
presented(value: Any, context: PresentationContext | None) -> Any

One value as the serializer's .data, under the context of the call it belongs to.

None is presented as None: it is JSON's null, and a serializer handed none renders a row of blank fields indistinguishable from a real one.

docs.title: DRF permission classes off HTTP
docs.text:
DRFPermissionCheck asks each class in order against the offline request and view built for the principal. The first refusal raises NotPermitted with that class's message and code.

Before the class-level check, view.kwargs is filled from the call's arguments with what a route would have captured: every declared UrlKwarg, taking its default when the argument is absent or null, and the arguments the spec's row lookup reads. A declared QueryParam goes to request.query_params. The object check asks only about model instances. A create or a collection is never asked about an object, as on HTTP.

docs.title: DRFPermissionCheck
docs.text:
Bases: PermissionCheck

DRF permission classes asked the kernel's three questions, off HTTP.

The kernel asks a principal and a spec; a DRF permission class asks a request and a view. So each question asks every class in order, a fresh instance each time, as a DRF view's get_permissions does, against the request and view the call carries, else the offline pair build_offline_context builds for the principal. The first refusal raises the dual-base NotPermitted with that class's own message and code, so a client is told what a DRF view would have told it; returning False instead would leave the kernel to raise its own class with the generic wording.

The view's kwargs are filled from the call's arguments before the class-level check. A permission scoping by a route capture reads view.kwargs["project_pk"] in has_permission, and off HTTP there is no URLconf to put it there; asked against an empty mapping it would refuse every caller it means to admit. Each method opts in to the kernel's arguments channel by declaring the keyword, and the names that go onto view.kwargs are the ones a route would have captured: every declared UrlKwarg, and route_reads, the arguments the spec's row lookup reads (pk of an update's instance lookup, or of a retrieve), which as_kernel_spec passes in. Each declared QueryParam goes onto request.query_params instead, where a query string would have put it. A UrlKwarg or QueryParam the call left out, or sent as null, takes its declared default, as its docstring says a transport seeds it, and is otherwise absent. Where a transport asks with no arguments at all (None), nothing is filled, and the classes decide what an empty route means, as they would for a URL that captured nothing.

The request and view the call carries come first. The class-level and object-level methods declare request and view, so a call registering either as a seed hands it over, and call_context, so a call that puts either in its context does: a transport running the kernel's dispatch carries the request a run arrived on, or a role view built for the operation, that way. Each is the seed, else the context's entry, and None in either place is no value. A carried view, or DRF Request, is asked as it is, with nothing filled onto it. Where the call carries one and not the other, the missing half is the offline pair's, built as below, so no class is ever handed None for a request or a view; where it carries neither, the whole offline pair is asked. The offline view's action is the call's context's action, where that is a non-empty string, so a class branching on view.action reads the operation's name; a carried view keeps its own. A carried Django request that DRF has not wrapped, the request a run arrived on as the kernel's call context holds it, is asked as a DRF Request around a copy of it, built as the offline pair is: its user the principal and its query string the declared QueryParam values the call sent, replacing its own, which is the endpoint's the run arrived on. Asked with no arguments at all, nothing is routed and its own query string stays. On drfs' own edge the kernel asks no check, since dispatch_spec runs under the Grant its view's permission classes produced.

has_object_permission asks only about a model instance, as enforce_permissions always has off HTTP; any other target is allowed here, because a DRF class written for a row reads attributes off it.

has_scope_permission allows. The kernel asks it of a bulk call's set, a collection's rows and a create's None, and DRF has no such question: on HTTP, a create and a collection action run the class-level check and no object check, and a DRF has_object_permission handed a QuerySet or None would raise AttributeError or decide on the wrong object. The class-level check has already run, with the view's kwargs filled, by the time the kernel asks this one.

No state is kept between questions: the compiled spec holding this check is shared by every call and every thread, so each question builds its own request and view.

docs.title: NotPermitted
docs.text:
Bases: NotPermitted, PermissionDenied

A permission check refused the principal, as both the kernel's NotPermitted and DRF's PermissionDenied.

Every published consumer of this package catches DRF's PermissionDenied by name and ends the attempt on it, and DRF's exception handler answers it 403. None of them catches the kernel's class, so a denial dispatch makes leaves as this, and an except written against either side catches it.

Deliberately not a service error, which the kernel's class is not either: an agent reads a service refusal as something to route around and keeps trying, where a denial should end the attempt.

message is the kernel's, and detail is the same words as DRF's ErrorDetail, coded "permission_denied" unless code is given.

Both __init__s run by name, so neither depends on the order of the bases, which is a choice (the kernel's first, as the class is named) and no test can tell from the other. The kernel's sets message: test_the_default_is_the_kernels_message fails without it. DRF's sets detail with the code given, which the kernel's super() chain never passes: test_a_code_given_is_kept fails without it.

docs.title: build_offline_context
docs.text:
build_offline_context(
    user: Any,
    params: Mapping[str, Any] | list[Any] | None = None,
    *,
    http_request: HttpRequest | None = None,
    action: str | None = None,
    kwargs: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    query_params: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    host: str | None = None,
) -> OfflineContext

Build the OfflineContext for dispatching a spec outside an HTTP request.

dispatch_spec forwards request / view to spec callables (kwargs providers, extend_queryset, context providers) that declare them, and enforce_permissions needs a request + view to evaluate permission_classes. This synthesizes both so a spec written for the HTTP transport keeps working when driven from a Pydantic-AI toolset, the MCP server, a management command, or a task runner.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default user Any

Set as request.user, so callables and permissions that read it behave as on HTTP.

required params Mapping[str, Any] | list[Any] | None

Seeds request.data, straight into DRF's parsed-data cache (a synthetic request has no stream to parse). It is not validated here — that is dispatch_spec's job, which takes params directly and never touches request.data. Pass both the same value.

None http_request HttpRequest | None

An ambient Django request to wrap, so its headers / META are available (the MCP server passes its real one); otherwise an OfflineHttpRequest is created. Either way the method is forced to POST, because mutation callables often branch on it. The caller keeps ownership: a request passed here is never written to. What gets wrapped is a shallow copy, so the method / GET / user this function sets land on the copy alone, while META, the session, the upload handlers and any body already read stay shared — headers and session writes behave as they do on HTTP, and the live request keeps its own method, query string and user for the rest of its cycle. Pass the request you are serving; dispatching several specs from one request is safe, and neither leaks into the next.

None action str | None

The view action name, exposed on the OfflineServiceView.

None kwargs Mapping[str, Any] | None

The channel for route-derived values — the off-HTTP counterpart of a view's URL captures. dispatch_spec spreads it into the selector / target pools exactly where the HTTP path spreads extra_url_kwargs=view.kwargs: authoritative over params on a key conflict, below a spec.kwargs provider, which also sees it as view.kwargs. Pass every route capture a spec depends on.

None query_params Mapping[str, Any] | None

Seeds the request's GET QueryDict, the source request.query_params reads — how read-shaping params that are not spec inputs reach the serializer offline: a serializer branching on query_params, and a request-scoped FilterSet reading self.request.query_params itself. It is not what a filter_set is bound to: dispatch_spec binds a SelectorSpec's own, and a target lookup's, to filter_data, else to params, and a service's output_selector_spec.filter_set to filter_data, else to an empty mapping (always to an empty mapping under output_filter_from_call=False). To filter from this query string, pass filter_data=context.request.query_params. Values are stringified as on HTTP; a list / tuple becomes a multi-valued param. Replaces a wrapped http_request's GET — on the copy that is wrapped, so the caller's own GET still reads its real query string afterwards.

None host str | None

The origin the synthesized request reports, so build_absolute_uri — which DRF's FileField / HyperlinkedIdentityField call whenever a request is in the serializer context — returns real absolute URLs off HTTP. Accepts "example.com", "example.com:8000", or a full origin whose scheme decides whether links are https. There is no default: unset, absolute-URI building degrades to the relative URL rather than raising (see OfflineHttpRequest). Ignored when http_request is supplied, whose own headers are authoritative, so a caller can pass both unconditionally.

None

docs.title: The kernel's refusals as DRF's
docs.text:
The kernel raises its own InvalidArguments, NotPermitted and PrincipalUnavailable, which neither DRF's exception handler nor a transport catching DRF's ValidationError or PermissionDenied knows. The edge runs the kernel inside translate_dispatch_errors(), so what dispatch_spec and adispatch_spec raise for a kernel refusal is one of the three classes below, each both the kernel's refusal and DRF's: an except written against either package catches it, detail carries ErrorDetails with their codes, and DRF answers it 400 or 403. The one refusal that is DRF's alone is a many spec's rows sent as a bare list, answered as DRF's list serializer answers them, with a plain rest_framework.exceptions.ValidationError: a body that is no list, a refused row, a row's undeclared key, or more rows than the bound. So catch DRF's ValidationError for every refused argument.

A caller running the kernel's dispatch, resolve_target or shape_queryset itself, or calling apply_queryset_shaping, gets the kernel's classes and wraps the call in the same block where it wants DRF's.

A deactivated principal is PrincipalUnavailable, a 403.

docs.title: translate_dispatch_errors
docs.text:
translate_dispatch_errors() -> Generator[None]

Re-raise the kernel's DispatchErrors inside the block as this package's dual-base classes.

Every published consumer of this package catches DRF's ValidationError and PermissionDenied by name, and DRF's exception handler answers only those; the kernel's own refusals reach none of them, and a view serves one as a 500. So the DRF edge runs the kernel's dispatch inside this block:

  • the kernel's InvalidArguments leaves as InvalidArguments, with the same tree and every message's code;
  • its NotPermitted as NotPermitted, and its PrincipalUnavailable as PrincipalUnavailable, each with the same message;
  • a subclass of any of the three leaves as that class's twin, with the subclass's message.

The new exception is raised from the kernel's, so the traceback keeps where dispatch refused. Each dual-base class is still the kernel's, so an except DispatchError around the block catches what leaves it as well.

Left exactly as raised:

  • anything that is not a DispatchError, a service's own refusals among them;
  • a DispatchError that is already a DRF exception, such as a dual-base class a validator raised itself, which both ladders already catch;
  • a DispatchError with no twin here, which keeps the kernel's class rather than be given a DRF answer nobody declared.

Use it as a with block, around await too. Not as a decorator on an async def: that would wrap the creation of the coroutine, not its run.

docs.title: InvalidArguments
docs.text:
Bases: InvalidArguments, ValidationError

The arguments were refused, as both the kernel's InvalidArguments and DRF's ValidationError.

Every published consumer of this package catches DRF's ValidationError by name - an MCP server answering "invalid arguments", an agent tool asking the model to retry - and DRF's exception handler answers it 400. None of them catches the kernel's class, so what dispatch refuses leaves as this, and an except written against either side catches it.

Deliberately not a service validation error, which the kernel's class is not either: a business rule stated by a service about well-shaped input is a different refusal, and an MCP server answers the two differently.

detail is the kernel's tree - fields, nested objects, rows under their int index - with every message an ErrorDetail. A message that carries a code (the kernel's CodedMessage does) keeps it, and one that carries none takes code, "invalid" unless given.

DRF's __init__ runs on purpose. By the order of the bases the kernel's runs, and it leaves detail as plain strings: DRF's handler still answers 400 with a byte-identical body, but get_codes() raises, so a test asserting the body passes on the broken class. test_get_codes_keeps_the_kernels_code_and_defaults_the_rest and test_every_message_is_an_error_detail are what fail without it.

docs.title: PrincipalUnavailable
docs.text:
Bases: PrincipalUnavailable, PermissionDenied

The principal cannot act, as both the kernel's PrincipalUnavailable and DRF's PermissionDenied.

Raised for an identifier naming nobody or a deactivated account, before any permission check. It reaches every published consumer's ladder as the denial DRF names, answered 403 and ending the attempt, and an except written against the kernel's class catches it too.

Deliberately not a service error, which the kernel's class is not either: a refused principal is terminal, never something to route around.

message is the kernel's, and detail is the same words as DRF's ErrorDetail, coded "permission_denied" unless code is given. The default is the kernel's wording, not DRF's, since there is nobody to refuse a permission to.

Both __init__s run by name, as NotPermitted's do, so the order of the bases is a choice no test can tell from the other. The kernel's sets message: test_the_default_is_the_kernels_message_not_drfs fails without it. DRF's sets detail with the code given, which the kernel's super() chain never passes: test_a_code_given_is_kept fails without it.

docs.title: register_drf_row_errors
docs.text: A nested write's row service written for DRF refuses its row with DRF's ValidationError. Registered, which dispatch_spec's module does when it is imported, that refusal lands at its row, {"books": {1: {...}}}, with its codes, and is still DRF's ValidationError.

docs.title: register_drf_row_errors
docs.text:
register_drf_row_errors() -> None

Register DRF's ValidationError as a refusal the kernel re-roots under the row that raised it.

A nested write runs a row service per related row, and one written for DRF refuses its row with DRF's ValidationError, which the kernel cannot name, so it would otherwise escape the write naming no row. Registered, it is re-addressed as the kernel's own refusals are - a collection's row under its int index, a message about the row itself under non_field_errors - and rebuilt as DRF's ValidationError, with every message's code kept, so DRF still answers it 400.

Process-wide and for the life of the process, as the kernel's registry is. Running it again does nothing, because the reader is one module-level function; a second registration of the class with any other reader is refused by the kernel.

Not a home for this package's dual-base InvalidArguments: the kernel reads its own InvalidArguments before any registered class, so that one leaves a nested row as the kernel's class, and reaches DRF's ladders through translate_dispatch_errors.

docs.title: as_kernel_spec
docs.text:
as_kernel_spec(
    spec: Any,
    *,
    partial: bool | None = None,
    spread: bool = False,
    seeded: frozenset[str] = frozenset(),
) -> KernelServiceSpec | KernelSelectorSpec

Compile spec, a drfs ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec, to the kernel's.

What each drfs spec's own as_kernel_spec() answers, so the kernel's entry points - dispatch, authorize, the registry and the schemas - take a drfs spec as it is; they read it through kernel_spec, which compiles it once per object. This function compiles afresh on every call.

Each field lands on one seat:

  • input_serializer becomes the SerializerValidator, and the output serializer the SerializerPresenter, with the spec's field_audiences layered over the serializer's markings. A ServiceSpec's output serializer is its output_selector_spec's; one whose selector is None re-reads nothing, so it compiles to no output selector, and its serializer is the compiled spec's own presenter. Where that output is a LIST and the spec is not many, the service returns the rows, which compiles to returns_many=True: the kernel presents the return row by row and describes it as an array of the row.
  • permission_classes becomes one DRFPermissionCheck; an empty sequence, which drfs reads as "no permissions, explicitly", becomes [Unrestricted()], the kernel's spelling of the same; None compiles to no permissions, which the kernel's registry and dispatch refuse, so a drfs spec reaches a transport without a view only guarded.
  • reads is what the selector and the target lookup take, and under spread what a service with no input_serializer takes, read off their signatures as spec_to_json_schema reads them: named parameters and the keys of an Unpack-ed TypedDict, with InputRequired read as required and a NotClientInput key on any callable of the call left out. A named parameter with no default is required too, as the callable raises TypeError without it, unless a kwargs provider that says nothing of its keys may fill it or the callable is a wrapper that fills its own (_reflected). A row handed in as dispatch(target=...) does not excuse its lookup's key on this compile: the kernel checks the arguments before it reads the target, so a caller handing one still sends the key. The DRF edge's per-request variants (kernel_spec_variant) leave optional exactly the reads this rule requires (required_for_having_no_default), so a view handing the row it resolved, and each refusal stage the edge documents, answer as they always did. A misplaced marker is refused here, so at registration. Each declared UrlKwarg and QueryParam in the spec's own reads is a Parameter too, winning over a reflected one of its name, required where the read says so or the parameter it replaces is (a read declaring a default is not: _merge), and a read unless it is a shape (below); one the target lookup reads joins the lookup's reads. Every read taken off a signature is marked reflected and a declared one is not, so the kernel fills a registered pool seed's name in the former on every dispatch, kernel_spec(spec)'s included, and still refuses the latter as an argument meeting a seed (test_the_kernel_fills_a_selector_s_reflected_read_from_the_seed, test_a_declared_read_named_like_the_seed_is_still_refused_by_the_kernel).
  • shapes is each declared QueryParam of the top-level spec that no callable of the call takes by name: not the service or selector, a precondition, a target lookup, a kwargs or input_data provider, a bare **kwargs or a filter_set field. It shapes what is rendered, as a serializer reading ?fields= does, so the kernel hands it to the presenter alone, on PresentationContext.shapes, rather than to a callable. One a callable names stays in reads, and so does a nested spec's own. A name the filter_set reads is the filter's, as the filter field always won the schema. The pool's own names (user, request, view, serializer and the kernel's reserved seeds) are never arguments, and a declared one is refused. So is a declared read the service or selector, or one of its preconditions, marks NotClientInput: dispatch would hand that callable the client's value under the name it keeps the server's. A name only a target lookup hides is not refused; the lookup is never handed it, and the read is the service's argument. A route capture no signature names and no UrlKwarg declares is no argument at all, so it no longer reaches a spec.
  • The rest carries by name: atomic, idempotent, many, many_argument, allow_none, affordances, kwargs, input_data, preconditions, progress_reporter, metadata, select_related, prefetch_related, annotations, filter_set. many takes the bounds of the list serializer DRF builds for the input_serializer. extend_queryset, which drfs calls as (queryset, view, request), is wrapped so the kernel, which binds it by name, calls it the same way; view and request are then the pool's registered seeds. A SelectorSpec's affordances map to the compiled form of each ServiceSpec.

partial overrides the spec's own for the variant the DRF edge builds per request (PATCH); None reads the spec's, where only True is partial. A spec with no input_serializer has nothing to relax, so it compiles unpartial.

spread is ArgumentBinding.SPREAD_AUTHOR_WINS: a service with no input_serializer then takes the caller's values for its own parameters. Without it, as AUTO and BUNDLE dispatch a service, a caller fills only what the Validator, the target lookup and the declared reads read, so def destroy(*, instance, hard=False) is never handed a hard the request sent (see _takes_its_signature).

seeded names seeds a dispatch registers beyond the pool's own, and leaves a signature's parameter of such a name - the selector's, a target lookup's, a spread service's - out of the compiled reads altogether (test_seeded_compiles_a_name_out_of_a_selector_s_reads_a_marked_read_stays, test_seeded_compiles_a_name_out_of_a_target_lookup_s_reads, test_seeded_compiles_a_name_out_of_a_spread_service_s_reads). Without it the parameter is a reflected read, which the kernel fills from a registered seed of its name on every dispatch but which stays among the compiled reads. The DRF edge no longer passes seeded. A declared read of the name stays one, which the kernel refuses as an argument meeting a seed.

What the kernel refuses at construction is stripped or refused here, naming the drfs field. Stripped, because drfs never read them: an output selector's kwargs, an instance lookup's allow_none (the kernel would resolve a missing row to None, an upsert, where drfs answers 404), a nested spec's permission_classes and a target lookup's output_serializer. Refused, as drfs refuses them at as_view(): a nested selector's preconditions and progress_reporter, which would never run. Also refused: a selector of None anywhere but an output selector or an instance lookup, which compiles to no lookup, and field_audiences with no output serializer to layer them over.

success_status, document_service_error and response_finalizer are the HTTP views', and none of them is carried. input_serializer_context rides on the SerializerValidator and output_serializer_context on the SerializerPresenter, which hands it the value it presents as result for a service's output and as instance for a retrieve.

docs.title: kernel_spec_variant
docs.text:
kernel_spec_variant(
    spec: Any,
    *,
    partial: bool | None = None,
    unguarded: bool = False,
    target: bool = False,
    server_input: bool = True,
    spread: bool = False,
    lenient: bool = False,
    excluded: frozenset[str] = frozenset(),
) -> KernelServiceSpec | KernelSelectorSpec

spec compiled as one request of the DRF edge dispatches it, once per variant.

With every keyword at its default this is kernel_spec(spec), the one compiled spec every kernel entry point reads. Each other combination is compiled once per source object and kept while it lives, so a request never recompiles and a Grant minted for a variant covers it on the next call too.

Each other combination is the edge's, and it leaves optional every read kernel_spec(spec) requires only for having no default: the edge fills such a parameter from a row a view hands in, and refuses a missing one at the stage it documents, the target lookup's or the service's own (test_the_edge_s_variant_relaxes_exactly_the_reads_the_rule_asks_for). InputRequired, a required TypedDict key and a declared read saying required=True stay required; a declared read that does not is relaxed as the parameter it names would be.

  • partial: the per-request flag a PATCH sets, compiled by as_kernel_spec; None reads the spec's own.
  • unguarded: no permissions. An HTTP view has already run DRF's check_permissions, so the edge hands dispatch a Grant and the compiled checks would only be asked again against a synthesized request.
  • target: a service spec that declares no target lookup gets a stand-in instance lookup, so the edge can hand dispatch(target=...) the row the view's get_object() resolved; the kernel refuses target= on a spec with no target selector. The stand-in reads no arguments and is never called: a dispatch reaching it raises ImproperlyConfigured. A spec with a target lookup keeps its own.
  • server_input: False compiles the spec with no kwargs provider of its own and, on a service spec, no input_data: the DRF edge evaluates both itself and merges what they answer into the arguments, and a service spec's kwargs seat hands back the author values the edge call carries (author_values) instead. Leaving either on would call the provider a second time (test_a_provider_runs_once_per_call, test_the_input_data_provider_runs_once_per_call).
  • spread: a service spec with no input_serializer takes the caller's values for its own parameters, as an explicit ArgumentBinding.SPREAD_AUTHOR_WINS dispatches it. Off by default, as AUTO and BUNDLE dispatch a service, so kernel_spec(spec) declares none of them.
  • lenient: a service spec's Validator declares its fields by name alone (SerializerValidator(lenient=True)), so the kernel's shape check passes each value through to the serializer. The edge compiles this for a request a live DRF view dispatches, which DRF's serializer has always answered alone: a form's "on" for a boolean, 123 for a string, every field's refusal at once, in DRF's words. A caller off HTTP keeps the kernel's typed check. A many spec's list is unbounded there too, so its ListSerializer alone bounds a live view's body, as DRF's view always did: a body past the kernel's SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH is taken where the list serializer declares no max_length, and one past a declared bound is refused in DRF's words.
  • excluded: names a service spec's Validator declares no parameter for (SerializerValidator(excluded=...)): the edge compiles the names a seed of the call takes, so a serializer field of that name is the serializer's alone rather than a parameter the kernel refuses.

docs.title: Protocols
docs.text: Each Protocol is parameterised by input, instance (where applicable), and result. **extras is typed Any, so the framework's kwargs pool flows through without the service having to declare each key. Strict-typed extras live on the user's function signature via **extras: Unpack[YourKw] — see Typing services and selectors for the full pattern.

docs.title: CreateService
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol[InputT, ResultT]

The structural shape of a service that takes validated input and no target.

data is what the spec's Validator returned, under the pool's reserved data seed. **extras absorbs whatever else the keyword pool delivers - user, a registered seed, the spec's kwargs - without the service declaring each key. It is typed Any so a service conforms under every type checker.

Nothing reads the Protocol at run time: dispatch binds a service from the keywords it declares whatever it is annotated with, so conforming is a claim checked by a type checker, through implements.

Strictly typed extras stay possible on the service's own signature: declare them as a TypedDict whose keys are all NotRequired and annotate **extras: Unpack[YourExtras], so extras["tenant"] is typed in the body. NotRequired because the Protocol's caller may not supply them. The Protocol carries no type argument for the extras, since that cross-check is not portable across type checkers.

docs.title: UpdateService
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol[InputT, InstanceT, ResultT]

The structural shape of a service that acts on a resolved row with validated input.

instance is the row the spec's instance_selector_spec resolved, under the pool's reserved instance seed, and data what the spec's Validator returned.

See CreateService for **extras and strictly typed extras.

docs.title: DeleteService
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol[InputT, InstanceT, ResultT]

The structural shape of a service that acts on a resolved row, input optional.

instance is the row the spec's instance_selector_spec resolved. Most deletes return None.

data has a default in the Protocol, so a service that reads no input conforms without declaring it: bind InputT to NoInput and leave data out. A delete that does take input - a reason, a confirmation - binds InputT to its input type and declares data with a default of its own, data: ReasonInput | None = None: declared without one it does not conform, since the Protocol's caller may leave data out.

See CreateService for **extras and strictly typed extras.

docs.title: create_model
docs.text:
create_model(
    model: type[ModelT],
    *,
    field_map: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    exclude_fields: list[str] | None = None,
    m2m: Mapping[str, Any] | Callable[[Any], Mapping[str, Any]] | None = None,
    relations: Mapping[str, RelationSpec] | None = None,
) -> Callable[..., ModelT]

A service that builds a row of model from its validated data, and returns the row.

The service a create operation would otherwise write by hand:

def create_author(*, data: AuthorIn, **_: Any) -> Author:
    return create_from_input(Author, data).instance

field_map, exclude_fields and relations are handed to create_from_input as they are, so one relations map writes every nested kind, a reverse foreign key's ChildSpec among them. m2m is a static mapping, or a callable handed the validated data that returns one, which is the usual case when the rows to link arrive in the arguments:

create_model(Post, m2m=lambda data: {"tags": data.tags})

The service returns the row, not the ChangeResult, since the row is what a create's output presents. It opens no transaction: dispatch runs a service inside one, which covers the row and every nested write. It takes **kwargs, so the rest of the pool - the user and any registered seed - is absorbed rather than refused. It names call_context, which a catch-all is never handed, and the same pool with the call's context beside it is handed on as the helper's context, so a row service a relation spec declares can see who is calling and, by naming call_context, the very dict the call's other stages share.

docs.title: update_model
docs.text:
update_model(
    model: type[ModelT],
    *,
    field_map: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    exclude_fields: list[str] | None = None,
    m2m: Mapping[str, Any] | Callable[[Any], Mapping[str, Any]] | None = None,
    update_fields: bool | list[str] = True,
    relations: Mapping[str, RelationSpec] | None = None,
) -> Callable[..., ModelT]

A service that writes the validated data onto the resolved row, and returns the row.

The service an update operation would otherwise write by hand:

def update_author(*, instance: Author, data: AuthorIn, **_: Any) -> Author:
    return update_from_input(instance, data).instance

model is not read: it is taken for symmetry with create_model and to bind the row's type for a type checker, since the row is the instance the spec's instance selector resolved. field_map, exclude_fields, update_fields and relations are handed to update_from_input as they are, and m2m is read as create_model reads it.

The service returns the row rather than the ChangeResult, opens no transaction of its own, absorbs the rest of the pool and hands it on as context with the call's context beside it, as create_model's does.

docs.title: delete_model
docs.text:
delete_model(
    model: type[ModelT],
    *,
    soft_delete: Callable[[ModelT], None] | None = None,
    relations: Mapping[str, RelationSpec] | None = None,
) -> Callable[..., None]

A service that deletes the resolved row, after the rows it owns, and returns None.

The service a delete operation would otherwise write by hand:

def delete_author(*, instance: Author, **_: Any) -> None:
    instance.delete()

model is not read, as in update_model: the row is the instance the spec's instance selector resolved.

soft_delete is called with the row instead of instance.delete(), for a row that is retired rather than removed:

def archive(instance: Author) -> None:
    instance.is_archived = True
    instance.save(update_fields=["is_archived"])

delete_model(Author, soft_delete=archive)

So no row is deleted and Django sends no pre_delete or post_delete for it.

relations is the map the writes take, and what it declares goes before the row, deepest first, through delete_relations: the rows the instance owns are disposed of, a many-to-many loses its membership, and a forward relation is left alone. It is the cascade a database will not run - a PROTECT foreign key, or a soft delete, which removes no row for Django to cascade from - and the one a declared delete_service sees row by row. A value that is not a relation spec is refused with ImproperlyConfigured here, when the service is built, rather than at its first call. With no map, or an empty one, nothing but the row is touched.

The service opens no transaction: dispatch runs it inside one, so a refused cascade leaves every row in place. It absorbs the rest of the pool and hands it on, with the call's context it names, as the cascade's context, so a row's delete_service can see who is calling and, by naming call_context, the very dict the call's other stages share.

Deletes with await instance.adelete(), after the cascade adelete_relations runs by the rule delete_model states. soft_delete is an async def called with the row in place of adelete().

docs.title: delete_collection
docs.text:
delete_collection(
    model: type[ModelT], *, soft_delete: Callable[[Any], None] | None = None
) -> Callable[..., None]

A service that deletes the resolved collection in one bulk delete, and returns None.

Pairs with a spec's collection_selector_spec, whose rows dispatch seeds into the pool as collection. The service a bulk delete would otherwise write by hand:

def delete_books(*, collection: QuerySet[Book], **_: Any) -> None:
    collection.delete()

collection.delete() is Django's bulk delete, which runs each foreign key's on_delete and sends pre_delete and post_delete for every row, as a single row's delete does. An empty collection deletes nothing, so running the operation twice is harmless. model is not read, as in delete_model.

soft_delete is called with the collection instead of delete(), as in lambda rows: rows.update(is_archived=True). The service opens no transaction, since dispatch runs it inside one, and absorbs the rest of the pool.
